extracted.intended_audience: aspiring orators, speechwriters, and students of rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and delivering public speeches in the classical (Ciceronian/Attic) tradition: choosing style, ornament, figures, delivery, and argument appropriate to subject, speaker, and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orator's three purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: An orator must so speak as to 'prove, delight, and force the passions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To 'prove' is necessary (logical demonstration); to 'delight' is required to engage attention (style, beauty); to 'force the passions' secures victory (moving the audience). These three aims guide choice of elocution and rhetorical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match elocution to purpose (three kinds of elocution)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three kinds of elocution: 'the neat and accurate' used in proving; 'the moderately florid' used in delighting; and 'the vehement and impetuous' used in forcing the passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine which part of the speech or which cause requires which elocution and temper between them. Each part of an oration or entire causes may need different management using these styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorum / becomingness (to prepon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain propriety of character — adapt language and sentiments to what's becoming given the nature of subject, the speaker's and hearers' characters, time, place, and occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid loftiness for trivial matters and avoid puerile triviality for grave matters. Consider speaker rank, age, audience, antagonist; 'what is becoming' differs from 'what ought to be' and governs suitability rather than moral perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excess and defect; observe the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Every thing has its proper mean; excess is more offensive than a proportionable defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of exaggeration or deficiency in sentiment or expression (Apelles' criticism of contemporaries who never knew when they had performed enough).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-consistent voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep character consistent: do not put the language of a worthy man into the mouth of a ruffian, or that of a wise man into the mouth of a fool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors and painters maintain character; an orator must likewise adapt diction and expression to the character being spoken for or representing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and Attic modesty (Atticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Attic (simple and easy) speaker imitates conversation: modest simplicity, plainness, free and unconfined language that is pure, correct, clear, and perspicuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appear 'at ease' without 'glitter of ornament.' Use 'industrious negligence'—naturalness achieved by labour. Intermix lively sentiments sparingly; be sparing in new words and cautious with antiquated words. Avoid conspicuous ornament and studied prettiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled use of metaphors and tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors and tropes may be used when resemblance is obvious or to express something without a proper name, but must not be too conspicuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain metaphors that occur in conversation (e.g., fields are 'thirsty') suit the simple Orator. Avoid bold, conspicuous metaphors in the simple style and reserve the most striking tropes for loftier elocution. Examples and named tropes: metaphor, metonymy, hypallage, catachresis, allegory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornaments of language and sentiment — use appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornaments of language: single-word choices and word-order figures; ornaments of sentiment: elevated turns of thought. Both are valid but must fit the style/persona.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'single word' is well chosen when it sounds agreeable and best expresses meaning. Word-order figures should not betray design; sentimental ornaments lose nothing by changing word order. Reserve the more conspicuous ornaments for more elevated species of Eloquence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-studied figures and verbal artifices in Attic style
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not employ conspicuous figures like contracting word to word, identical cadences, artful letter-changes or play of sound that betray an obvious design to please.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Attic/simple mode, these studied prettinesses are out of character. Repetitions requiring forceful vocal exertion are also inappropriate in this lower style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middling (temperate) eloquence: richer ornament and melodic flow
rubrics_metrics.description: A middle species is fuller and richer than the Attic: all ornaments of language may be employed without reserve; the flow is soft and harmonious and suited to elaborate topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This style supports a 'brilliant, florid, picturesque, and well-wrought Elocution' and is often the offspring of philosophic training. Use metaphors and tropes more freely, following exemplars like Demetrius Phalereus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majestic / copious / nervous eloquence — use with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: The grand, copious, and majestic orator bends and sways the passions with sonorous, rapid, and diffusive language, but if untempered by simplicity and moderation this style becomes contemptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This style must be balanced with the simpler and middle characters; a speaker who only amplifies and exaggerates without clarity, calmness, or humour will appear to rave or vapour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility across topics and parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A finished Orator should be able to speak about trivial subjects with simplicity and art, on weighty ones with energy and pathos, and on middling matters with calmness and moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt style within a single speech as required; intermix the three characters. Examples: Cicero's different causes and Demosthenes' varied orations illustrate versatility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wit and humour — prohibitions and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sorts of wit: smart repartees and humour. Both may enliven speech but must be limited to avoid scurrility, indecency, petulance, inhumanity, misplaced levity, and unseasonable use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid affected witticisms (dragged from the closet), jesting upon friends or persons of quality, ill-natured strokes, attacking the unfortunate, or making light of atrocious crimes. Aim jests mainly at enemies and with consideration of character, time, and place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness; avoid affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid affected witticisms or expressions that seem contrived; natural and occasional expression is preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affected devices appear cold and insipid. A design too evident to please (e.g., over-contrived phrasing or theatricality) undermines decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in gesture and facial expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Gesture should be neither pompous nor theatrical but moderate and easy; much efficacy comes from countenance which must correspond to sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stiff or affected countenance; delivery must harmonize with language and the speaker's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misapplied ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule must not be used too often, indecently, petulantly, against the unfortunate, against atrocious crimes, or unseasonably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misapplied ridicule leads to scurrility, buffoonery, ill-breeding, or censure for inhumanity. Use ridicule sparingly and appropriately targeted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of words and syntax (linguistic precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: The orator should understand the force, extension, and different species of words both singly and in sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of lexical categories and sentence structure is foundational; this connects to the need for logical training and accurate expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of logic and argumentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A finished Orator should master the art of Logic insofar as it applies to public speaking, since oratory and disputation are both forms of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study Aristotle and dialectical methods; apply logical method to strengthen proofs ('to prove') while using eloquence to diffuse and ornament argument. Balance reasoning (logician’s close method) with eloquence (more diffusive mode).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of lexical innovation and archaisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sparing in new-made words and cautious with obsolete (antiquated) words — they may be proper but are rarely used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use neologisms and archaisms only when they suit character or needed ornament; excessive use harms naturalness and may appear affected.
